deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Euler's own proof ("demonstratio mea") of the four-square divisor theorem. It follows Krafft's proof on p.197. Lemma I (p.197): if gcd(N,n)=1, any integer can be written Nx+ny with |x| ≤ n/2. Lemma II (p.197) is Euler's four-square identity with A=aα+bβ+cγ+dδ, B=aβ−bα−cδ+dγ, C=aγ+bδ−cα−dβ, D=aδ−bγ+cβ−dα. The setting carried over from p.197: N is a prime with N | P²+Q²+R²+S². The roots are reduced to |p|,|q|,|r|,|s| < N/2, so Nn = p²+q²+r²+s² < N² and n < N. Then p=Na+nα, …, s=Nd+nδ with |a|,…,|d| ≤ n/2 (Lemma I, valid because gcd(N,n)=1). Expanding gives Nn = N²(a²+b²+c²+d²) + 2NnA + n²(α²+β²+γ²+δ²). Since n ∤ N², it follows that n | a²+b²+c²+d².

PAGE 198, part 1 (end of the four-square descent).
(1) Put a²+b²+c²+d² = n n'. Since each |a_i| < n/2, the sum is < n², so n' < n (unless n=1).
(2) Divide by n: N = N²n' + 2NA + n(α²+β²+γ²+δ²).
(3) Multiply by n': Nn' = N²n'² + 2Nn'A + nn'(Σα²).
(4) Replace nn' by Σa² and apply Lemma II: nn'Σα² = A²+B²+C²+D².
(5) Hence Nn' = N²n'² + 2Nn'A + A²+B²+C²+D² = (Nn'+A)² + B²+C²+D².
(6) So Nn' is again a sum of four squares, with n' < n. Iterating gives Nn'', Nn''', … with strictly decreasing multipliers, which must reach N·1. So N is a sum of four squares. Q.E.D.

PAGE 198, part 2 (two-square analogue, claimed to be 'easier than hitherto').
Theorem: a sum of two coprime squares admits only divisors that are themselves sums of two squares.
Lemma: (a²+b²)(α²+β²) = A²+B² with A=aα+bβ, B=aβ−bα.
Proof:
(1) Take Nn = p²+q², and write p=Na+nα, q=Nb+nβ with |a|,|b| < n/2. Then a²+b² < n²/2.
(2) Nn = N²(a²+b²) + 2Nn(aα+bβ) + n²(α²+β²). Put a²+b² = nn'. [Implicit: n | a²+b² because gcd(N,n)=1.]
(3) N = N²n' + 2NA + n(α²+β²).
(4) Multiply by n': Nn' = N²n'² + 2Nn'A + nn'(α²+β²) = (Nn'+A)² + B², with n' < n/2.
(5) Descent reaches N·1, so N = x²+y².

PAGE 198, part 3 (start of 'Alia demonstratio simplicior', finished on p.199).
Claim: if any N divides P²+Q²+R²+S², with no single term divisible by N, then N is a sum of four squares.
I. Write P = 𝔄N ∓ p etc. with p,q,r,s < N/2. Each square is then < N²/4, the sum p²+q²+r²+s² < N² is divisible by N, and the quotient n < N.
II. Nn = p²+q²+r²+s². Write p = a+αn, …, s = d+δn, i.e. reduce directly mod n rather than via Na+nα.
The continuation on p.199 gives Nn' = (n'+A)² + B²+C²+D² with n' < n. This is the now-standard modular-reduction descent.
errors: Lemma I's assertion that one can always reach |x| < n/2 (strict) is false for even n: the residue n/2 gives |x| = n/2. So Σa² ≤ n², not < n², is all that is justified. The descent does not actually stall. If n is even and all four residues equal ±n/2, then p,q,r,s are odd multiples of n/2, so n² | Nn and hence n | N. That is impossible for prime N > n ≥ 2. Euler leaves this case unaddressed.
The case n' = 0 is not discussed. In the prime-N proofs it is harmless: a=b=c=d=0 forces n | N, hence n=1, the terminal case.

Two-square part: the step 'Nn divisible by n, hence n | a²+b²' silently requires gcd(N,n)=1. So does Lemma I's representation p = Na + nα. The argument is therefore valid only for prime N (or N coprime to every multiplier arising), not for the stated divisors of arbitrary coprime sums of two squares. It also implicitly needs N not to divide both p and q.
Two-square part: from |a|,|b| ≤ n/2 one gets a²+b² ≤ n²/2, so n' ≤ n/2 rather than strictly less. This is harmless for the descent.

'Simpler' proof for arbitrary N: the hypothesis 'no single P,Q,R,S divisible by N' does not prevent n' = 0, so the descent can break. Example: N=8, P=Q=R=S=2 gives 16 = 8·2. Each term is not divisible by 8, but n=2 divides every root, so all a_i = 0, n' = 0 and Nn' = 0 (step finished on p.199). The conclusion stays true, since 8 = 2²+2², but the proof needs a gcd hypothesis, e.g. gcd(n,N)=1, at each stage. So Corollary 1 on p.199 ('etiamsi N non fuerit numerus primus') is not justified as written.

results.what: Completion of the descent proof that a prime N dividing a sum of four squares (not all divisible by N) is itself a sum of four squares, via the identity Nn' = (Nn'+A)² + B²+C²+D² with n' < n
results.modern_name: Euler's descent step in the proof of Lagrange's four-square theorem (four-square divisor lemma)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (E242, 1751/1760, divisor theorem); full theorem Lagrange 1770; Euler's simplified proof E445 (1772/1774)

results.what: Euler's four-square identity with a particular sign pattern (conjugate form)
Descent proof that a prime dividing a sum of two coprime squares is a sum of two squares, via Nn' = (Nn'+A)² + B², n' ≤ n/2
results.modern_name: Euler's descent for the two-square theorem (Fermat's Christmas theorem, divisor step)

results.what: Simplified descent reducing the roots directly mod n (p = a + αn) instead of p = Na + nα
results.modern_name: Standard textbook descent proof of the four-square theorem

deep.surprise_reason: All material is Euler's well-known descent method for the two- and four-square theorems, which appears in his published papers (E241, E242, E445). The page is a draft or alternate version of known work. The only point of minor interest is the explicit side-by-side comparison with Krafft's proof and the overreaching claim for composite N.
